items.prompt: Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise on hot days. What is hot weather here?
choices: A shared cause (confound)
A reverse cause of both
A mere coincidence of trends
items.explanation: Hot weather independently pushes both numbers up, so they move together without either causing the other.

items.prompt: A city with more police also has more crime, because high crime led it to hire police. What pattern is this?
choices: A hidden confound
Pure coincidence
Reverse causation
items.explanation: The arrow runs from crime to police, opposite to the obvious reading.

items.prompt: Which check tests for reverse causation?
choices: Compare within weather groups
Which of the two changed first
Ask who benefits from the claim
items.explanation: Causes come before effects, so the timeline can rule a direction in or out.

items.prompt: Two unrelated trends both rise over the same ten years and nobody can explain a link. What pattern is this?
choices: A confirmed cause
A measured confound
Likely coincidence
items.explanation: With no mechanism and only a shared drift over time, the match is most likely an accident.

items.prompt: Does a strong correlation tell you why two things move together?
choices: No, only that they move together
Yes, one of them causes the other
Yes, but only in one direction
items.explanation: Correlation describes the pattern. The reason needs a separate check.

items.prompt: How do you test a suspected confound?
choices: Collect many more data points over several years
Compare within groups of the shared cause
Report the correlation more precisely
items.explanation: Holding the shared cause fixed shows whether the link survives without it.

items.prompt: Which is the stronger claim?
choices: That two things move together
They are equally strong claims
That one thing causes the other
items.explanation: Causation needs a mechanism and ruling out other explanations, not only a pattern.

items.prompt: Umbrella sales and traffic accidents both rise on rainy days. What explains the link?
choices: Umbrellas cause accidents
Rain pushes both of them up
Accidents cause umbrella sales
items.explanation: Rain is the shared cause, so banning umbrellas would change nothing about accidents.

items.prompt: Children with more books at home score higher on reading tests. A parent plans to buy 200 books to raise a child's score. Which check best separates a shared cause from a real effect?
choices: Compare similar households with different book counts
Measure the correlation to many more decimal places
Survey twice as many families from the same town
Check whether every test score was recorded accurately
items.explanation: Households with more books likely differ in many ways. Comparing similar households asks whether books matter once those shared factors are held fixed.
items.reference:
Three ways a real correlation misleads
confound: a shared cause drives both (rain: umbrellas and accidents)
reverse causation: the arrow runs backwards (crime: more police)
coincidence: no mechanism, only a shared trend
fixes: compare within groups, check the timeline, ask for a mechanism
Why: each pattern has its own fix, and a correlation coefficient cannot tell them apart.
items.learnMore:
Confound, reverse causation, coincidence

A correlation says two quantities move together. A confound drives both, reverse causation flips the arrow, and coincidence has no link at all. Compare within groups, check which changed first, and ask for a mechanism.

Common mistake

Making the correlation stronger or the sample bigger. That firms up the pattern but says nothing about why it exists.
items.reflection: Think of two things in your own life that rise and fall together. What third factor could be driving both?

items.prompt: Hospitals that use ventilators more often have higher death rates. Which reading is a shared cause rather than ventilators causing deaths?
choices: Ventilator use is recorded wrongly in some hospitals
Hospitals with low death rates stop using ventilators
Sick patients get ventilators and also die more
Ventilators were bought in the same year as new beds
items.explanation: Severity of illness drives both ventilator use and death, so the two rise together without a direct cause.

items.prompt: What is the base rate of fake coins in a batch with 2 fakes per 100 coins?
choices: How common fakes are, 2%
How often the machine is right, 98%
How often it beeps, 2%
items.explanation: The base rate is how common the real thing is before any test is applied.

items.prompt: What does the true positive rate measure?
choices: The share of beeps that are real
The share of genuine coins left alone
The share of real cases it catches
items.explanation: It conditions on the case being real and asks how often the signal fires.

items.prompt: What does the false positive rate measure?
choices: The share of real cases that are missed
The share of non-cases flagged anyway
The share of beeps that are fakes
items.explanation: It conditions on a genuine coin and asks how often the machine beeps anyway.

items.prompt: What does precision measure?
choices: The share of real cases that are caught
The share of coins that are fake
The share of signals that are real
items.explanation: It conditions on the signal having fired and asks how often it was right.

items.prompt: Out of 1,000 coins with a 2% base rate, how many are fake?
About 5% of 980 genuine coins wrongly beep. How many false beeps is that?
19 fakes beep and 49 genuine coins beep. How many beeps in total?
items.explanation: Every beep counts, real or not: 19 plus 49.

items.prompt: When the real thing is rare, a beep from a 95% accurate machine is often what?
choices: Almost certainly a real fake
More often false than real
Real about 95% of the time
items.explanation: A small false positive rate on a huge pool of non-events produces more false beeps than true ones.

items.prompt: Out of 10,000 coins, 1% are fake. A machine beeps at 90% of fakes and at 10% of genuine coins. About what share of beeps are fakes?
choices: About 90%
About 8%
About 45%
About 10%
items.explanation: Fakes: 100, caught 90. Genuine: 9,900, false beeps 990. Real beeps are 90 of 1,080, about 8%.
items.reference:
Accuracy versus precision at a 2% base rate
1,000 coins: 20 fake, 980 genuine
fakes that beep: 19 (95% of 20)
genuine coins that beep: 49 (5% of 980)
beeps that are real: 19 of 68, about 28%
Why: a small false positive rate on a huge pool of non-events outweighs a high true positive rate on a tiny pool of real ones.
items.learnMore:
The base rate calculation

Precision is the real beeps divided by all beeps. Count real beeps as base rate times true positive rate, false beeps as the remaining share times the false positive rate, then divide. The rarer the real thing, the more false beeps dominate.

Common mistake

Reading the machine's accuracy as the chance that a beep is real. Those are two different conditional probabilities.
items.reflection: Think of a warning or test you trust because it is 'usually right'. How common is the thing it warns about?

items.prompt: Two alerts both catch 95% of real events and falsely fire on 5% of non-events. One watches an event at a 20% base rate and the other at 0.5%. Which statement is true?
choices: The 20% alert's beeps are far likelier real
Both alerts' beeps are equally likely to be real
The 0.5% alert's beeps are more likely to be real
Neither can be compared without more rates
items.explanation: Precision depends on the base rate as well as the error rates, so identical detectors can differ hugely in how far a firing can be trusted.

Raising the true positive rate to exactly 100%
Cutting the false positive rate from 5% to 1%
Adding a second dashboard showing the alert
items.explanation: Almost every firing comes from the huge pool of non-events, so the false positive rate sets precision. A better true positive rate barely moves it.

items.prompt: Comparing within weather groups holds what fixed?
choices: The weather itself
The ice cream eaten
The sunburn rate
items.explanation: Inside one group weather is the same for everyone, so it cannot explain a difference there.

items.prompt: What does random assignment do to other factors?
choices: Removes them from the whole dataset
Measures each of them
Spreads them evenly across groups
items.explanation: A coin flip decides who is treated, so other factors cannot decide it.

items.prompt: After splitting by weather, the gap is 0 in both groups. What explains the original gap?
choices: The ice cream itself
The mix of weather days
An error in the measurement
items.explanation: Weather accounted for the whole gap seen at the start.

items.prompt: Which evidence is strongest for a causal claim?
choices: A larger sample of observations
A very strong correlation
A randomly assigned comparison
items.explanation: Random assignment handles confounds nobody listed, which adjustment cannot.

items.prompt: Hot days show 40% sunburn with ice cream and 40% without. What is the gap within hot days?
choices: 0 points
18 points
6 points
items.explanation: Both groups are at 40%, so the difference is zero.

items.prompt: What is a natural experiment?
choices: A study run in a natural park
An outside event shifting one variable
A trial where subjects pick their own group
items.explanation: Something outside the researcher's control shifts one variable for unrelated reasons.

items.prompt: What does mechanism plausibility add to a claim?
choices: Proof that the effect really exists
A larger sample of similar cases
A concrete cause-to-effect chain
items.explanation: A believable chain supports the claim but does not prove it.

items.prompt: Splitting by weather can only remove confounds of what kind?
choices: Every possible confound
The ones someone recorded
Those that are small
items.explanation: Adjustment only covers factors someone recorded and included.

items.prompt: Coffee drinkers have 16.8% heart problems against 7.2% for non-drinkers. Smokers have 20% in both groups and non-smokers 4% in both. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Coffee does cause heart problems, though smoking causes far more of them
Smoking and coffee use must be completely unrelated
The measured gap proves nothing and the data is unusable
Smoking explains the gap; coffee shows no effect within groups
items.explanation: Inside each smoking group the gap is zero, so the mix of smokers accounts for it. Unmeasured factors could still matter.
items.reference:
From adjustment to experiment
compare within groups: removes the confounds you measured
a gap of 0 inside every group: the measured factor explains it
random assignment: balances measured and unmeasured factors
proxies: natural experiment, before/after with comparison, mechanism
Why: only randomisation cuts every arrow into the cause, including the ones nobody listed.
items.learnMore:
Controlling and experiments

Splitting data by a suspected confound shows whether a gap survives inside each group. Random assignment goes further because it balances factors nobody measured. When it is impossible, natural experiments, comparison groups and mechanisms are weaker substitutes.

Common mistake

Treating a gap that vanished after one adjustment as proof of no effect. It only shows the measured factor explains the gap.
items.reflection: Think of a claim you have heard that rests on a comparison. What could the groups differ in besides the thing being compared?

items.prompt: Why can a randomised comparison support a causal claim where adjustment cannot?
choices: It uses a larger sample than any observation
It balances factors nobody thought to measure
It removes every source of random noise
It guarantees the result will be statistically significant
items.explanation: Random assignment makes treatment independent of everything else, measured or not. Adjustment only handles what was recorded.

items.prompt: Implement `expectedFakes(total, baseRate)`: how many of `total` coins are fake, rounded to a whole number.
items.explanation: The base rate is the share of coins that are fake, so the count is total times base rate.

items.prompt: Implement `falseBeeps(genuine, falsePositiveRate)`: how many genuine coins wrongly beep, rounded to a whole number.
items.explanation: The false positive rate applies to the genuine coins only.

items.prompt: Implement `caughtFakes(fakes, truePositiveRate)`: how many fakes beep, rounded to a whole number.
items.explanation: The true positive rate applies to the fakes only.

items.prompt: Implement `precisionFromCounts(realBeeps, falseBeeps)`: the whole-number percentage of beeps that are real. Return 0 if nothing beeped.
items.explanation: Precision is real beeps over all beeps. With no beeps at all, return 0 instead of dividing by zero.

items.prompt: Implement `totalBeeps(realBeeps, falseBeeps)`: every beep counts, real or false.
items.explanation: The machine cannot tell which beeps are real, so the total is the sum of both kinds.

items.prompt: Implement `percentOf(part, whole)`: the whole-number percentage that `part` is of `whole`. Return 0 if `whole` is 0.
items.explanation: A rate is a count divided by the group size, and an empty group needs its own answer.

items.prompt: Implement `gapPoints(rateA, rateB)`: how many percentage points `rateA` is above `rateB` (negative if below).
items.explanation: Within a group where both rates match, the gap is 0 points.

items.prompt: Implement `isMostlyReal(precisionPercent)`: true when more than half of the beeps are real.
items.explanation: More than half means strictly above 50, so exactly 50 does not count.

items.prompt: Implement `alertPrecision({ baseRate, truePositiveRate, falsePositiveRate })`: the percentage of alerts that are real, rounded to one decimal place (for example 27.9). Return 0 when no alert can fire.
items.explanation: Real alerts come from the events that happen and are caught. False alerts come from the non-events that fire anyway. Precision is the real share of the sum, with a guard for when neither can occur.
items.reference:
Turning counts into code
real beeps = base rate * true positive rate
false beeps = (1 - base rate) * false positive rate
precision = real / (real + false)
guard the case where nothing beeps at all
Why: the same arithmetic as the coin table, written once so any base rate can be tried.
items.learnMore:
Precision as a function

The coin-machine table is a formula in disguise. Write it as a function of three rates and call it across base rates, and the collapse of precision for rare events becomes something you can compute directly.

Common mistake

Dividing without a guard. When the base rate is 0 nothing real can beep, and a false positive rate of 0 can make the denominator zero too.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you make from a test result. If you wrote it as a function of base rate and error rates, what inputs would you need to find?
